content_voiceover: This slide shows ABO grouping two ways, the classic tube method and the gel or column agglutination card. In the tube method, forward typing mixes the patient's red cells with known anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D reagents; reverse typing mixes the patient's serum with known A1 and B reagent cells. Here anti-A is 4 plus, anti-B is 0, anti-D is 4 plus, A1 cell is 0, and B cell is 4 plus. Cells agglutinate with anti-A but not anti-B, giving forward type A; serum agglutinates B cells but not A1 cells, confirming reverse type A. Anti-D positive means Rh positive, so this patient is A positive. The gel card runs the same panel in six columns, and you read strength by how far cells migrate through the gel after spinning. Key board point: forward and reverse typing must always agree, and any mismatch signals an ABO discrepancy that needs workup.
keypoints: Forward typing tests patient RBCs against known anti-A, anti-B, anti-D reagents.
Reverse typing tests patient serum against known A1 and B reagent cells.
Forward and reverse results must match; a mismatch means ABO discrepancy.
Gel card, or CAT, gives the same result, read by agglutinate position after centrifugation.
keypoint_voiceover: Forward typing tests the patient's red cells against anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D. Reverse typing tests the patient's serum against known A1 and B reagent cells. In this example, both point to type A positive. Always confirm forward and reverse typing agree, a mismatch is an ABO discrepancy that needs further workup, whether you use the tube method or a gel card.
